lesson_title: Owing R400: Why the Inequality Sign Flips
hook_text: Everyone memorises the flip rule. Nobody believes it — until the debt collector explains.
clip_script: Having R400 beats having R250 — obviously. Now flip both into debt: OWING R400 versus OWING R250. Which position wins now? Owing R250, without question. The bigger number became the worse position the moment it crossed into debt. In symbols: four hundred is greater than two hundred and fifty, but minus four hundred is LESS than minus two hundred and fifty. That is the entire rule. Multiplying or dividing by a negative drags every amount through zero into debt, and the comparison must turn over with it. So when minus three x is greater than twelve crosses your page, dividing by minus three gives x is LESS than minus four. And memory is never your only defence: minus three times minus five is fifteen, bigger than twelve — it works.
visual_style: Two wallets morphing into two red debt slips as they swing across a giant zero on a number line, the inequality sign physically rotating; a green tick stamps the test value at the end.
pacing: Fast wallet setup, a heavy flip beat as the amounts cross zero, calm certainty on the test.
